lead: Sentiment analysis finds attitude in text: positive, negative, neutral or an emotion. It exists because no team can read a lakh UPI app reviews by hand. A lexicon scores known opinion words; a classifier learns weights from labelled reviews. Banks use it on complaint tweets, film teams on song reviews, product teams on feedback. This chapter covers binary, multi-class and aspect-based sentiment, lexicon scoring with negation and intensifiers, machine learning on text features, and evaluation with precision, recall and F1.
prereq: You need: 5.1 for bag-of-words and TF-IDF, 5.2 for Naive Bayes, logistic regression and SVM, and 5.3 for features and metrics.

blocks.text: Binary sentiment gives one label: positive or negative. Multi-class sentiment adds neutral or a 1-to-5 star scale; stars are ordinal, so confusing 1 with 2 is a smaller error than 1 with 5. Emotion labels such as joy and anger are related, but speech emotion recognition belongs to Unit 7.

Aspect-based sentiment keeps the target. “The film is dull but the songs are excellent” gives film negative and songs positive. One overall positive score hides the film complaint. Aspects are entities or features: film, songs, battery, delivery, refund. Each gets its own polarity.

Labels must match the decision. “Not bad” is often positive, while “bad” alone is negative. A factual review such as “delivery arrived on Tuesday” is neutral, not positive. With 90 percent positive reviews, accuracy 90 percent may only match always saying positive; use per-class metrics from 5.3.

A lexicon maps words to polarity scores. Simple scale: good = +2, excellent = +3, bad = -2. SentiWordNet-style lexicons store positive, negative and objective scores for each word sense, so meaning matters; see Unit 4 on WordNet senses.
Score in four steps: tokenize; find opinion words; apply negation and intensifiers; add scores. Basic sum:

blocks.where: score(s) is total polarity; p(w_i) is the lexicon score of token w_i; neg_i is -1 when a negator such as not scopes over w_i, else +1; int_i is 1.5 for very, 0.5 for slightly, else 1. Scores are dimensionless.

blocks.text: Negation flips the next opinion word: not good = +2 × -1 = -2. Intensifiers scale: very good = +2 × 1.5 = +3. Contrast words such as but and however change weight; a simple rule halves the clause before but and keeps the clause after. Drop objective words, which add noise.

Lexicons need no training data and are easy to explain. They fail on domain shift: unpredictable is bad for a banking app and good for a thriller. They also miss sarcasm and implicit complaints such as “I waited two hours”.

Machine learning treats sentiment as text classification. Label reviews positive, negative or neutral. Convert each review to bag-of-words or TF-IDF features plus word and character n-grams (5.1). Mark negation as one token, so not_good is a feature. Train Naive Bayes, logistic regression or SVM (5.2).

Naive Bayes is fast and works on small data; it assumes independent features, so treat it as a baseline. Logistic regression gives probabilities and readable weights. A linear SVM handles sparse high-dimensional text well and maximises the margin. For multi-class, use one-vs-rest or softmax.

A few hundred labelled reviews per class can beat a lexicon in one domain, because the model learns local words such as refund and crash. The cost is annotation and overfitting. Use cross-validation; tune smoothing for Naive Bayes and C for logistic regression and SVM, as in 5.3.

sections.h3: Evaluation with precision, recall and F1

blocks.text: Test on held-out labelled reviews. For positive as the class of interest: TP = predicted positive and truly positive; FP = predicted positive but negative; FN = truly positive but predicted negative. Then:

blocks.where: P is precision, the share of predicted positives that are correct; R is recall, the share of true positives found; F1 is their harmonic mean. TP, FP and FN are counts, so P, R and F1 are proportions.

blocks.text: Report per-class P, R and F1, not only accuracy. For aspects, compute P, R and F1 separately for film, songs and battery. Macro-F1 is the unweighted mean of aspect F1 values and exposes a weak rare aspect; micro-F1 pools decisions and favours frequent aspects. State which one you report.
Use a confusion matrix to see which classes are confused, especially neutral. For star ratings, add mean absolute error. Compare against a majority-class baseline.

spec.aria: Token boxes not, good, but, excellent, songs with lexicon scores, an arrow from not flipping good; a number line from minus 3 to plus 3 with film at minus 2, songs at plus 3 and the whole review at plus 1.

examples.question: A lexicon gives good = +2, excellent = +3, bad = -2. The negator not multiplies the next opinion word by -1. Use only the negation rule; treat but as neutral. Score “not good but excellent songs” and give the aspect view: film negative, songs positive. Show every intermediate value.
steps: Tokens are: not, good, but, excellent, songs. Opinion words are good and excellent; not negates good; but is neutral; songs is an aspect.
For good: p(good) = +2, neg = -1, so score = +2 × -1 = -2.
For excellent: p(excellent) = +3, no negator in scope, so score = +3.
Total score = -2 + 3 = +1. Total is greater than 0, so the review is positive.
Aspect view: film gets -2, which is negative; songs gets +3, which is positive. The total hides these opposite signs.
examples.answer: Total score is +1, so the review is positive; film is -2 negative and songs are +3 positive.
examples.check:
good = 2
excellent = 3
not_good = -1 * good
exc = excellent
total = not_good + exc
print(not_good)
print(exc)
print(total)

traps: Ignoring negation: not good is -2, not +2; check the scope of not.
Assuming domain independence: unpredictable is bad for banking and good for thrillers.
Reporting one total when aspects disagree: film -2 and songs +3 average to +1 and hide the complaint.
Using accuracy on imbalanced data: 90 percent positive reviews make always-positive look strong.
Treating SentiWordNet sense scores as word-level scores: the same word can differ by sense.

quiz.a: It assigns polarity to a specific aspect, such as film or songs, not only to the whole review.

quiz.q: Why is negation handled before summing lexicon scores?
quiz.a: It flips the scoped word, so not good scores -2; adding +2 first gives the wrong polarity.

quiz.q: Lexicon: good = +2, bad = -2, not multiplies next by -1; very multiplies by 1.5. Treat but as neutral. Score “very good but not bad”.
quiz.a: very good = +2 × 1.5 = +3; not bad = -2 × -1 = +2; total = +5, so positive.

quiz.q: TP = 30, FP = 10, FN = 20. Compute precision, recall and F1.
Why report macro-F1 for aspect sentiment?
quiz.a: It weights each aspect equally, so poor performance on a rare aspect is visible; micro-F1 hides it under frequent aspects.

quiz.q: A model gets 92 percent accuracy on 1000 reviews, 900 positive. Why is this weak?
quiz.a: The majority baseline is 90 percent; the model is only 2 points better. Report per-class P, R, F1 and the confusion matrix.

quiz.q: Name two classifiers used for sentiment.
quiz.a: Naive Bayes and linear SVM; logistic regression is also common.

beyond: Not for the exam. Industry sentiment systems often combine a lexicon, a supervised classifier and an aspect extractor. Transformer models from Unit 6 now handle sarcasm and context better, but lexicons remain useful for explainability and low-resource languages. Search next for aspect-based sentiment analysis, SentiWordNet and cross-domain sentiment. Speech emotion recognition is a separate problem in Unit 7.
